questions.q: A scanner reports a server has CVE-2024-1234 with a CVSS of 9.8, and a second server with no CVEs but admins log in over plain telnet with a shared password. Which do you worry about, and why?
options: Both - the misconfigured telnet box is at least as dangerous, and attackers often prefer misconfigs since they need no exploit and raise no alert
Only the CVE box - a high CVSS always wins
Only the telnet box - CVEs are never exploited
Neither - no CVE means no risk
questions.exp: Ch.1: misconfigurations are at least as important as CVEs and are often preferred. CVE = the bug's name, CVSS = its 0-10 score.

questions.q: You have valid administrator credentials for a fully patched, properly configured Windows box. Can Metasploit still get you in?
options: No - patching blocks all Metasploit access
Yes - known admin creds let Metasploit give you a Meterpreter shell even on a hardened box
Only if there's an unpatched CVE
questions.exp: Ch.1: credentials beat configuration. This is the whole setup for the book.

questions.q: You land a Meterpreter session but 'getuid' shows a low-privileged user. What's true about what you can do and where you can go?
options: What you can see depends on your process's privileges, and you can migrate from a higher-privileged process down to lower ones
Meterpreter can't do recon until you're admin
You can migrate from low privilege up to SYSTEM for free
questions.exp: Ch.2: data available depends on the host process's privileges; migration goes high->low. Meterpreter lives in a process in memory, which is why file scanning misses it.

questions.q: Scenario: your lure is a tiny buffer overflow with almost no room for code, and later you phish a laptop on flaky hotel wifi that may drop after one connection. Which payload type for each, and why?
questions.answer: Tiny space -> STAGED (small stub downloads the rest). Flaky one-shot network -> STAGELESS (whole payload ships at once, needs no second connection).
questions.exp: Ch.3 exam favorite. Name tell: slash = staged (meterpreter/reverse_tcp), underscore = stageless (meterpreter_reverse_tcp).

questions.q: Your payload needs to call home through a corporate firewall that blocks inbound connections. Bind or reverse?
options: Reverse - the target connects out to you (LHOST/LPORT), and outbound is usually allowed
Bind - the target listens and you connect in
questions.exp: Ch.3: reverse beats firewalls/NAT. A handler catches the callback; run it as a job (exploit -j) in the background.

questions.q: You need to brute force one service and have limited time. The book says which targets/services are faster, and what 4 things define the attack?
questions.answer: Windows is faster than Linux, and SMB is faster than SSH (Windows Wins, SMB is Speedy). The 4 features: userlist, wordlist, time, defenses (Users Want Time Delays).
questions.exp: Ch.4. Modules: smb_login and ssh_login. Defenses = lockout, rate limiting, MFA, strong passwords.

questions.q: You phish a user and they type the WRONG password into your fake Windows prompt. What happens with phish_windows_credentials?
options: It accepts anything and logs the wrong password
It keeps re-prompting until the credentials actually validate against the system
questions.exp: Ch.5: that re-prompt is why it works. You can run it from an UNPRIVILEGED session to steal the logged-on user's domain/local creds.

questions.q: You generated a payload and ran it through Metasploit encoders several times, but Defender still catches it. Why?
options: Encoders dodge bad characters, not AV - modern AV watches behavior, memory and the cloud
questions.exp: Ch.6/7: encoding != evasion. Whether malware runs depends on the target's AV; Windows ships Defender.

questions.q: You want to trojanize a real program so the victim sees normal behavior. Which tool and flags, and what does static vs dynamic analysis mean for the defender?
questions.answer: msfvenom with -x <real program> -k (keep it working), plus -p payload, -f format, -o outfile. Static = examine without running (strings, hashes, Ghidra). Dynamic = run and watch (strace, gdb).
questions.exp: Ch.6.

questions.q: You're admin on a box with Defender tamper protection ON. You can't disable Defender - what's your move for a lasting blind spot?
options: Disable Defender in the registry (still supported)
Add an exclusion - excluded paths/processes are never scanned, and admins can still add them even with tamper protection on
questions.exp: Ch.7: this is the key nuance. Quarantined threats can also be restored; registry-disable is no longer supported.

questions.q: You get a Linux shell and want your commands left out of history, and you notice '.' is early in the user's PATH. What do these two facts give you?
options: Only history matters, PATH is harmless
Only PATH matters, history can't be cleared
Hide tracks (unset HISTFILE / HISTSIZE=0 / set +o history) and hijack a command by dropping a fake binary that '.' in PATH runs first
questions.exp: Ch.1: PATH is THE security env var; attackers also suppress bash history. A shell also behaves differently by how it's started (login vs not).

questions.q: You find a second account in /etc/passwd with UID 0, and another account whose hash in /etc/shadow starts with '!'. What does each mean?
questions.answer: UID 0 = root, so that second account is a hidden root backdoor (Linux authorizes by UID, not name). '!' in front of the hash = the account is locked.
questions.exp: Ch.2. Account files: passwd, shadow, group, gshadow. Expired password = change at login; expired account = can't log in at all.

questions.q: You crack a hash from /etc/shadow that starts with $6$. What is it, and how did John get the password?
options: SHA-512, found by repeated guessing (hash a guess, compare) - hashes are one-way, not reversible
questions.exp: Ch.3: $1$=MD5, $5$=SHA-256, $6$=SHA-512, $y$=yescrypt. Salt = same password hashes differently per account, so rainbow tables fail.

questions.q: You can edit the sshd PAM stack. How do you get a shell on every SSH login attempt, even failed ones?
options: Add pam_exec.so - it runs your program during authentication regardless of success
questions.exp: Ch.3: pam_exec.so is the abuse; admins and attackers with privilege can edit PAM (/etc/pam.d).

questions.q: An attacker logged in via SSH and wiped one login record, but you still caught the login. Name the 3 record systems and why wiping one isn't enough.
questions.answer: utmp (who/w/last), lastlog (pam_lastlog.so), systemd (loginctl). Different programs write each, so scrubbing one leaves the login in the others.
questions.exp: Ch.4 (U-L-S). sudo is configured in /etc/sudoers via visudo; Polkit = elevation for the GUI.

questions.q: You see a process named 'nginx' using 100% CPU but the box doesn't run a web server. How do you confirm it's really an attacker's renamed binary?
options: Check /proc/<pid>/exe - it points at the real file on disk no matter what the process is named
Reboot and see if it returns
You can't - the name is authoritative
questions.exp: Ch.5: defenders hunt by name, so attackers rename; /proc/<pid>/exe defeats it. Talk to a process with signals: SIGKILL(9) can't be caught, SIGTERM(15) can.

questions.q: An attacker wants persistence that survives reboot on a systemd box. Where do they put it, and where do you look?
options: A malicious .service unit or timer in /etc/systemd/system; check systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled and list-timers
questions.exp: Ch.5: systemd is PID 1; admins and attackers both use it.

questions.q: You locked yourself out of a Linux box (lost root password) and separately find a SUID-root binary you don't recognize. What can you do with each?
questions.answer: Lost password: boot rescue/install media, mount the disk, chroot in, reset with passwd. Unknown SUID-root (find / -perm -4000): runs as root, so it's a privilege-escalation path or a planted backdoor shell.
questions.exp: Ch.6. SUID=run as owner, SGID=as group, sticky=only owner deletes (/tmp). Hard link=same inode; symlink=a path that breaks if target goes.

questions.q: A Red Hat box runs SELinux; an Ubuntu box runs AppArmor. One-line difference, and can both run at once?
options: SELinux = labels on everything, deny-by-default, tuned with Booleans; AppArmor = one profile per critical program; generally only one is active
They're identical and always run together
AppArmor labels everything; SELinux uses profiles
questions.exp: Ch.7: SELinux context = user:role:type:level (U aRe Totally Locked). Modes: enforcing/permissive/disabled; aa-logprof fixes an AppArmor profile from denials.

questions.q: You're told to make sure software on a Linux fleet is trustworthy. What two things matter most?
options: Repositories are valid (signed with trusted GPG keys) and installed files still match their package hashes (rpm -V, debsums)
questions.exp: Ch.8: apt=Debian/Ubuntu/Mint, dnf/yum=Red Hat/Rocky, zypper=SUSE. Snap/Flatpak bundle dependencies (but publisher patches them, not the distro).

questions.q: In a log you see powershell.exe launched with -EncodedCommand and a long Base64 string. What is happening, and why do attackers do it?
options: An obfuscated PowerShell command - Base64 hides keywords from simple command-line matching
questions.exp: Ch.1: Base64 and downloaded modules are the two obfuscation methods. PowerShell is the modern shell (runs on Linux too); cmd runs a registry AutoRun at startup and keeps history.

questions.q: You get cmd.exe to open and your command runs every time - you added a value in the registry. Which, and why do attackers like it?
options: The Command Processor AutoRun value - quiet user-level persistence inside a trusted program
The Run key only works for PowerShell
questions.exp: Ch.1: cmd executes AutoRun from the registry on startup.

questions.q: A domain group and a local group have the same name. A user is in the domain group - are they in the local group too?
options: Yes, same name means same group
No - different groups with different SIDs; domain membership doesn't grant local membership
Only if they share a RID
questions.exp: Ch.2: SIDs identify users/groups; well-known ones (S-1-5-18=SYSTEM, RID 500=Administrator) are the same everywhere. Local data=SAM, domain data=Active Directory.

questions.q: You dumped NTLM hashes but can't crack them in time. How do you still use them, and where did they come from?
questions.answer: Pass-the-hash: use the hash itself to authenticate instead of the password. They live in the SAM (local) and ntds.dit (domain); protected so even SYSTEM can't read them directly - you pull them as Administrator or Backup Operator.
questions.exp: Ch.3. Logon gives a login ID + access tokens; UAC lets you use a privileged token, controlled by registry/group policy.

questions.q: You download a flagged payload but want it to dodge the extra scrutiny Windows gives internet files. What do you do?
options: Zip it with a password only
Ship it inside a .iso or .vhd - those containers avoid the Mark of the Web
questions.exp: Ch.4: MOTW is stored in an NTFS alternate data stream (Zone.Identifier); copying to FAT32 also strips it. Windows files also have 8.3 short names and several timestamps.

questions.q: At a locked Windows login screen you press Shift 5 times and get a SYSTEM command prompt. What attack is this, what made it possible, and what defends against it?
questions.answer: Sticky Keys attack: you took ownership of sethc.exe (via SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege/SeRestorePrivilege) and replaced it with cmd.exe. Windows Resource Protection defends against it.
questions.exp: Ch.5. Security descriptor = Owner, Group, DACL, SACL, Flags (Only Good Dogs Sit First). DACL=access (Door), SACL=logging (Security camera).

questions.q: You want to see who can modify a service's files or a registry key. Which tools show the security properties/permissions?
options: icacls and Get-Acl, plus Sysinternals AccessChk/AccessEnum
questions.exp: Ch.5: File Explorer works but has subtle issues; SDDL = permissions as a string. Registry keys and values are securable objects with their own DACL (Ch.6).

questions.q: You see svchost.exe whose parent process is winword.exe, not services.exe. Why is that a red flag, and what trick might hide it?
options: svchost should be a child of services.exe - an odd parent signals injection/masquerade; attackers can spoof (obfuscate) a process's parent
questions.exp: Ch.7: defenders check the parent; attackers spoof it. Integrity levels (Low<Medium<High<System) drive UAC. Know the normal process tree.

questions.q: You find a service with an unquoted path 'C:\Program Files\My App\svc.exe' and you can write to C:\. How is this a privilege-escalation path?
options: Windows tries C:\Program.exe first, so your planted binary runs as the service's account at startup
questions.exp: Ch.8: unquoted service paths + weak permissions = escalation/persistence. Services run in the background via the Service Control Manager (sc, net, PsService, PowerShell); defined under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services. Accounts: LocalSystem > NetworkService > LocalService.

questions.q: Put a full attack in Cyber Kill Chain order using the book's tools: msfvenom payload, phishing email, handler/Meterpreter, AV exclusion, recon.
questions.answer: Recon -> Weaponize (msfvenom payload) -> Deliver (phishing) -> Exploit/Install (it runs, handler catches the callback) -> C2 (Meterpreter) -> Actions (recon, migrate, add AV exclusion to persist). Kill chain: Real Wizards Don't Exploit In Crowded Alleys.
questions.exp: Ties all books together. Misconfigs often beat CVEs as the way in.

questions.q: You need password hashes on both a Linux and a Windows box. Where is each, and what's the one-line difference in how users are identified?
questions.answer: Linux: /etc/shadow. Windows: SAM (local) + ntds.dit (domain). Linux identifies users by UID numbers (0=root); Windows by SIDs (RID 500=Administrator).
questions.exp: Linux Ch.3 + Windows Ch.3/Ch.2.

questions.q: Compare the 'extra lockdown' layer and the 'background program' persistence spot on Linux vs Windows.
questions.answer: Lockdown: Linux = SELinux or AppArmor; Windows = integrity levels (drive UAC). Background/persistence: Linux = systemd units/timers; Windows = services (Service Control Manager). Both used by admins and attackers.
questions.exp: Linux Ch.5/7 + Windows Ch.7/8.

questions.q: A defender asks how an attacker hides activity on each OS. Give the history/log trick for Linux vs Windows.
questions.answer: Linux: clear bash history (unset HISTFILE) and know logins sit in 3 places (utmp/lastlog/systemd). Windows: cmd history dies with the session, PowerShell PSReadLine file can be deleted, and Base64 hides the command's content; logons show in event 4624 with limits.
questions.exp: Linux Ch.1/4 + Windows Ch.1/3.
